title: Generating and downloading files (Blob + object URL); drag and drop; clipboard
summary: Build the content, wrap it in a Blob, and click an <a download> pointing at an object URL: that is a file export with no server. For Turkish Excel, write semicolons, decimal commas and a UTF-8 BOM, sorted with Intl.Collator("tr").

examples.title: A CSV writer for Turkish Excel, with Turkish sorting

annotations.note: Three rows need quoting: a quote inside a note, a semicolon, and a line break. Real exports always contain them eventually.
A column is a header plus an accessor. Generic over the row type, so toCsv works for any T and each accessor is checked against Order.
With Turkish settings the comma is the decimal mark, so Excel splits fields on semicolons. Numbers use the same convention: 1234,5 with no thousands separator.
The RFC 4180 rules with ; as the separator: quote a field that holds the separator, a quote or a line break, and double the quotes inside. Go's encoding/csv applies the same rules for you.
RFC 4180 ends lines with CRLF. The header row goes through cell() too, because header text can contain the separator as well.
Plain sort() compares UTF-16 code units, so Ç and Ş land after Z. Intl.Collator("tr") follows the Turkish alphabet: Ayşe, Çağla, Şule, Zeynep.
Only for display: the ⏎ marks each CRLF so the line endings are visible in the output. Line 38 is what goes into the file.
The whole download recipe: an object URL for the Blob, a temporary link with a download attribute, a click from code, then cleanup.
download works for same-origin, blob: and data: URLs. The name is a suggestion: browsers replace / and \ with _ and may adjust the rest.
An object URL keeps its Blob alive until revoked. A page that exports often and never revokes holds every export in memory.
Sandbox stand-in: the lesson iframe has no allow-downloads, so this listener cancels the click and reports what would be saved.
The BOM goes first, as its own part. The charset in the type matters when the Blob is opened in a browser tab, not to Excel.
37 UTF-16 code units become 45 bytes: Blob encodes strings as UTF-8, like a Go string. text() decodes as UTF-8 and drops a leading BOM, so check the bytes, not the text, when you test an export.

examples.title: A drop zone for CSV files, a copy handler, and the async Clipboard API

annotations.note: Elements reject drops by default. Cancelling dragover is what makes this one a drop target; without it, drop never fires.

Cancel drop too, or the browser may open the dropped file itself. dataTransfer.files holds File objects, the same type an input gives you. Filter by name: file.type is guessed from the extension and is often empty for CSV.
dispatchEvent and the browser call listeners synchronously and never await them. Keep the promise if anything must wait for the reading.
Synthetic events (isTrusted is false) run the same listeners, which is how this example and UI tests simulate a drop. dispatchEvent returns false when a listener cancelled the event.
A copy listener can replace what gets copied: setData, then preventDefault. Tab-separated rows paste into Excel as separate cells; semicolons don't split there.

navigator.clipboard.writeText is the modern API, but it needs a user gesture or a permission, and in an iframe a permissions policy too. Here it rejects with NotAllowedError, which real code must handle.

use_cases: Exporting the table the user is looking at, filtered and sorted, as CSV for Excel
Saving generated JSON, SVG or text reports without a server endpoint
Drop zones for CSV import, read with File.text() or stream() as in the reading-files lesson
Copy buttons and copy handlers that put spreadsheet-friendly, tab-separated text on the clipboard
strengths: A download takes three lines and no server: where a Go handler sets Content-Disposition, the page clicks an <a download>
Blob encodes strings as UTF-8 and reports the exact byte size, so a BOM or a size limit is easy to check before saving
File inputs, drag and drop and paste all deliver File objects, so one import function serves all three
weaknesses: The whole export is built in memory; for very large data, stream it from the server instead
The browser decides the download UX: it may prompt for a location or adjust the file name
Clipboard writes need a user gesture or permission, and synthetic events never count as one
There is no CSV writer in the platform: quoting and number formats are yours to get right

pitfalls.title: Comma-separated CSV for a Turkish Excel user
pitfalls.detail: With Turkish regional settings Excel splits on semicolons, so a comma-separated file opens as one column. Choose the separator per audience.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting the BOM
pitfalls.detail: Without it, Excel may read the file in the Windows code page and show Ã¼ for ü. Prepend "\uFEFF" for Excel-bound files only; other tools may keep it as part of the first header.

pitfalls.title: Never revoking object URLs
pitfalls.detail: Each URL keeps its Blob alive for the life of the document. Revoke once the download has started.

pitfalls.title: Not cancelling dragover
pitfalls.detail: drop never fires on an element that didn't cancel dragover, and an uncancelled drop lets the browser open the file.

pitfalls.title: Sorting Turkish text with sort() or the en collator
pitfalls.detail: Code-unit order puts Ç, Ö, Ş, İ after Z. new Intl.Collator("tr").compare follows the Turkish alphabet, with I before İ.

quiz.q: Your drop zone never receives drop events. What is missing?
options: A file input inside the zone
quiz.why: Elements reject drops by default; cancelling dragover is what makes one a drop target.

quiz.q: A Blob was built from ["\uFEFF", csv]. Does (await blob.text()).startsWith("\uFEFF") return true?
options: No: text() decodes as UTF-8 and strips a leading BOM
quiz.why: UTF-8 decoding removes the BOM. Read the first bytes with arrayBuffer() to confirm it is there.

quiz.q: With ; as the separator, how must the field zil bozuk; arayın be written?
quiz.why: A field that contains the separator, a quote or a line break must be quoted; inner quotes are doubled.

quiz.q: How should Çağla and Zeynep be ordered for a Turkish reader, and what produces that order?
quiz.why: Ç comes right after C in the Turkish alphabet; sort() compares code units and puts U+00C7 after Z.

body:
## Concept

A browser-side export has three steps: build the content, wrap it in a `Blob` with a
media type, and hand it to the browser through an **object URL** on an `<a download>` that
your code clicks. The browser then saves it like any other download. Nothing is uploaded.

CSV meant for a Turkish user's Excel needs a few deliberate choices: `;` as the separator,
a decimal comma, RFC 4180 quoting, UTF-8 with a byte order mark, and rows sorted with
`Intl.Collator("tr")`. Lines end in CRLF, as RFC 4180 and Excel's own CSV files have them,
though Excel reads LF too.

Microsoft documents the separator: the list separator comes from the Windows region
settings, and a comma decimal separator "forces Excel to use a semi-colon for the list
separator"
([Import or export text files](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/import-or-export-text-txt-or-csv-files-5250ac4c-663c-47ce-937b-339e391393ba)).
It also says a UTF-8 CSV opens normally "if it was saved with BOM"
([Opening CSV UTF-8 files correctly](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/opening-csv-utf-8-files-correctly-in-excel-8a935af5-3416-4edd-ba7e-3dfd2bc4a032)).
The rest was observed on 2026-11-14 with Excel for Microsoft 365 (build 16.0.20527.20196)
on an en-US Windows: double-clicked, a UTF-8 file without a BOM showed `Müşteri` as
`MÃ¼ÅŸteri` (its bytes read as windows-1252), and a BOM file with LF line ends opened
correctly. Tab-separated text pasted from the clipboard landed in separate cells, while
`;`-separated text stayed in one; the pasted `12,5` became the number 12.5 only with
Excel's decimal separator set to `,`.

The other direction reuses `File`. A drop hands you a `DataTransfer` whose `files` are the
same objects a file input gives you. The clipboard has two APIs: the synchronous `copy`,
`cut` and `paste` events, whose handlers read or replace `clipboardData`, and the
asynchronous `navigator.clipboard`, which needs a user gesture or a permission.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Go**: `encoding/csv` with `w.Comma = ';'` and `w.UseCRLF = true` does the quoting for
  you; the browser has no CSV writer, so `cell()` in example 1 is the whole library. On a
  server, `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=...` does what `<a download>` does.
- **Python**: `csv.writer(f, delimiter=";")` with `open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8-sig",
  newline="")` writes the BOM for you.
- **Java**: `OutputStreamWriter` with UTF-8 never writes a BOM; you write `\uFEFF`
  yourself, exactly as here.
- **JS/Node**: `fs.writeFile` takes a path. A web page never gets one: it can only offer a
  download, or ask the user for a file with `showSaveFilePicker()`, which only Chromium
  browsers implement.

## How it works

`URL.createObjectURL(blob)` registers the Blob in the document under a string such as
`blob:https://example.com/4f0c...`. As long as that URL is registered, the Blob can't be
garbage-collected; `revokeObjectURL` removes the entry. A `data:` URL is the alternative
for tiny files: the content is inside the URL string itself, so there is nothing to revoke,
but it grows with the content.

`new Blob(parts)` encodes string parts as UTF-8 and concatenates the bytes. That is why
`"\uFEFF"` becomes `EF BB BF`, and why `blob.size` counts bytes while `string.length`
counts UTF-16 code units.

## Design notes

Keep format decisions in one profile per audience. "CSV for Excel in Turkey" means
semicolons, decimal commas and a BOM. "CSV for machines", such as a Postgres `COPY ... CSV`
or a Go importer, means commas, decimal points and no BOM. Mixing the two is how a
`1234,5` turns into two columns.

Exported user text can contain cells starting with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@`. Excel turns such
a cell into a formula when the rest parses as one, quoted or not, so `=HYPERLINK(...)`
from another user becomes a live link. LibreOffice Calc's text import does it only with
its "Evaluate formulas" option checked
([LibreOffice help](https://help.libreoffice.org/latest/en-US/text/shared/00/00000208.html)).
When the data comes from other users, OWASP's
[CSV Injection](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/CSV_Injection) page recommends, for
Excel, a tab character at the start of such a field, inside its quotes. The older advice, a
single quote, shows in the cell, and OWASP calls it "not reliable in Microsoft Excel after
saving and re-opening the CSV file". Either prefix becomes part of the value, so a program
that reads the file back has to strip it again.

Observed on 2026-11-14 by opening a CSV in Excel for Microsoft 365 (build
16.0.20527.20196): `=1+1`, `+1+1`, `-1+1` and `@SUM(1,1)` became formulas, also inside
double quotes; `-5` stayed a number and `+90 532 000 00 00` stayed text. The tab-prefixed
and quote-prefixed cells stayed text, and still did after one save as "CSV UTF-8" and a
reopen.

Build exports in the browser when the data is already on screen and modest in size. For
large or sensitive exports, stream from the server instead: a Go handler writing through
`csv.Writer` straight to the response never holds the whole file in memory (the TraceLite
export step).
